scenarios.title: Tutorial: A Good Start with Leo
scenarios.topic: A friendly check-in: a strong reader whose reading log keeps coming back blank

prevalence.text: 33% of U.S. fourth graders performed at or above the NAEP Proficient level in reading in 2022.

why_address_it.text: "When schools, families, and community groups work together to support learning, children tend to do better in school, stay in school longer, and like school more."
why_address_it.source: Henderson & Mapp, A New Wave of Evidence (SEDL, 2002)

massachusetts.text: Massachusetts fourth graders' average NAEP reading score is consistently among the highest in the nation.

setting.meeting_context: A short, teacher-requested check-in after school on a Thursday in Room 108. Ms. Martins came straight from work and brought Leo with her. She seems glad to be here.

scenarios.teacher_concern: Leo's weekly reading log has come back blank or half-filled for three of the last four weeks, so he's missing the reading-log points on his report card. You'd like to agree on a simple routine at home.
scenarios.student_strength: BUT I notice Leo is one of the most enthusiastic readers in the room. He's always the first to volunteer during read-aloud, and last week he explained the ending of our chapter book to his whole table.

A.title: Leo's Reading Progress
A.summary: Leo reads above grade level and his fall-to-winter reading level went up two steps. Reading-log points: 1 of 4 weeks complete this month.

B.title: Weekly Reading Log
B.summary: Leo's log for the last four weeks: week 1 is full, weeks 2 and 3 are blank, week 4 has two nights filled in. Parent signature lines are empty.

parent_persona.name: Sofia Martins
parent_persona.personality: Warm, friendly and a little apologetic. She works as a dental hygienist and evenings are busy with Leo and his baby sister. She's proud of Leo and happy the teacher asked to meet. She wants to help and is easy to talk to.
parent_persona.speaking_style: Friendly and chatty, laughs easily, says 'oh, I know' and 'that's so him'. Asks practical questions.
knows: Leo loves to read, especially comics and dragon books.
The reading log goes home in his folder, but she doesn't always see it.
Evenings are hectic since the baby was born in the summer.
She thinks Leo is doing well in school.
hiding: She never really understood the log was graded; she thought it was optional.
She's a little worried Leo will struggle like his older cousin did, and she'd love ideas for how to keep him reading.
parent_persona.likely_claim: Leo reads every night, she's sure of it; they just forget to write it down.
softens_when: The teacher says something nice and specific about Leo.
The teacher asks about their evenings.
The teacher suggests something simple and practical.
escalates_when: The teacher makes it sound like she doesn't care about Leo's reading.

student_persona.name: Leo Martins
student_persona.personality: Cheerful, talkative, a bit shy at first with grown-ups in a meeting. Lights up when books come up.
student_persona.speaking_style: Short, excited sentences. Says 'um' a lot. Loves to name the book he's reading.
knows: He reads comics in bed with a flashlight most nights.
The log is at the bottom of his backpack and he forgets about it.
He is reading a dragon series and is on book three.
hiding: He reads under the covers after lights-out and is afraid he'll get in trouble for staying up.
student_persona.likely_claim: He does read. He just forgets the paper.
speaks_up_when: Someone mentions books, dragons, or read-aloud.

counselor.name: Grace Whitfield
counselor.title: School Counselor
counselor.knows: Knows Leo as a happy, well-adjusted kid. No concerns on file. Suggests praising the reading he already does and keeping any routine tiny.

nurse.name: Tom Aldana
nurse.title: School Nurse
nurse.knows: No health concerns on file for Leo. Mentions that eight-year-olds need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep, so a bedtime reading routine with a set lights-out can help.

principal.name: Janelle Ruiz
principal.title: Principal
principal.knows: The school counts reading minutes any way families can manage: a photo of the log, a quick note, or the class app. The log is meant to build a habit, not to punish.

colleague.name: Ben Castillo
colleague.title: Grade 3 teacher next door
colleague.knows: Has had luck letting students keep the log taped inside their book instead of in the folder, so it's there when they read.

scenarios.title: Chronic Absence: Maya
scenarios.topic: Student is repeatedly absent and missing content

prevalence.text: "The U.S. rate of chronic absenteeism ... decreased to 28% in the 2022-23 school year."

why_address_it.text: "Chronic absenteeism is the single strongest predictor of dropping out before graduation."

massachusetts.text: 17.1% of students were chronically absent in 2025-26, down from 22.2% in 2022-23.
massachusetts.source: DESE 2026 release, via Lynn Community TV

setting.meeting_context: Teacher-requested conference, Tuesday November 25, 2025, 3:15 PM, Room 214. Ms. Reyes left work early to be here. Maya came with her.

scenarios.teacher_concern: Maya has missed 14 days since September (9 of them unexcused) and signed in late 4 times. She is missing core Algebra I instruction, and her grade has dropped from a B+ to a D because of 11 missing assignments.
scenarios.student_strength: BUT I notice that when Maya is here, she's the first to finish the warm-up, her quiz average is a 91, and she helps the students at her table without being asked. She also mentioned she's been walking her little brother to school since her mom started early shifts.

A.title: 7-Day Absence Notification Letter
A.summary: Form letter dated October 20, 2025, mailed to the Reyes home at 18 Orchard Lane. States Maya has 7 absences, 5 of them unexcused, cites Massachusetts law (M.G.L. c. 76, § 1A) and PFPS Policy JH, and asks the family to call the Attendance Office to schedule a meeting to agree on action steps. No reply is recorded.

B.title: StudentView Attendance Summary
B.summary: Term 1 attendance through November 21: 14 absences (5 excused with a parent note, 9 unexcused) and 4 tardies to period 1. 12 of the 14 absences fall on a Monday or Friday. Maya's attendance rate is 76%, well below the 90% line for chronic absence.

C.title: Algebra I Progress Report
C.summary: Current grade 64 (D), down from 88 (B+) at the start of October. Quiz average 91. 11 missing homework and classwork assignments, most from days she was absent. Warm-up completion 100% on days present. Teacher comment: 'Strong reasoning; missing work is the issue.'

D.title: PFPS Policy JH: Student Attendance
D.citation: PFPS Policy JH, Sections 2-4; M.G.L. c. 76, § 1A
D.summary: Chronic absence means missing 10% or more of enrolled days for any reason. After 5 unexcused absences (M.G.L. c. 76, § 1A) the school must make a good-faith effort to reach the family by phone and mail and invite them to build an attendance plan together. Supports named in the policy: family liaison, transportation review, counselor referral, and referral to before- and after-school programs. The policy says the purpose is support, not punishment.

E.title: Automated Attendance Call Log
E.summary: All 9 automated absence calls since September 15 went to (413) 555-0192, which returned 'number not in service' every time. A contact update form Ms. Reyes submitted on September 8 with her new number, (413) 555-0347, was stamped received but never entered into StudentView. The school never actually reached her by phone.

delivery.subject: Re: Reyes contact info
delivery.body: I pulled the call log you asked about. The new number Ms. Reyes gave us in September never got entered, so every absence call went to a dead line. I'm so sorry. I'm fixing it right now.
delivery.notification: New message from Main Office · 1 attachment

F.title: Late Arrival Sign-In Sheet
F.summary: Maya's four late sign-ins, written in her own handwriting: 10/15 8:41 'overslept', 10/28 8:52 'missed bus', 11/12 9:10 'overslept', 11/19 8:38 'stopped at dunkin w/ friends'. The Route 6 bus log for 10/28 shows the bus arrived at 7:16 AM, two minutes early. None of the reasons mention the bus being late.

delivery.subject: Maya Reyes late sign-ins
delivery.body: Here is the scan you asked for.
delivery.notification: New message from Attendance Office · 1 attachment

parent_persona.name: Ana Reyes
parent_persona.personality: Warm but proud and exhausted. Since late August she has worked the 6:00 AM shift as a shift lead at the Pioneer Valley distribution center. Fiercely protective of Maya and afraid of being judged as a neglectful mother. Direct; gets clipped and cold when she feels talked down to. Relaxes quickly when someone treats her as a partner.
parent_persona.speaking_style: Plain, direct sentences. Bilingual; slips into a Spanish word or phrase ('mija', 'mira', 'ay') when emotional. Says 'with all respect' right before she disagrees.
knows: Maya has 'missed some days'. She thinks it is five or six, not fourteen.
Maya has complained about morning headaches.
A letter came from the school in October. She skimmed it and thought it was an automated form letter.
She has never received a single phone call from the school about absences.
She switched to early shifts in late August and leaves the house at 5:30 AM.
Maya's little brother Mateo is in grade 2 at Pemberton Falls Elementary.
hiding: She asks Maya to walk Mateo to Pemberton Falls Elementary every morning. The elementary school doesn't open its doors until 8:10, so Maya is late to high school or gives up and stays home.
When Mateo is sick, Maya stays home with him because Ana cannot lose shifts.
She is scared of losing her job if she asks her supervisor for a later shift.
She updated her phone number at the high school main office in September and assumed the school had it. She has not mentioned this yet.
parent_persona.likely_claim: Maya's lateness and absences are the bus's fault: the Route 6 bus is unreliable, comes late or skips the stop, so Maya misses it.
softens_when: The teacher names something specific Maya does well.
The teacher asks about the family's mornings instead of assuming.
The teacher offers concrete help (for example, a before-school program for Mateo) rather than consequences.
The school admits its own mistakes.
escalates_when: The teacher reads numbers at her without context or uses education jargon.
Anyone implies she doesn't care about Maya's education.
The teacher accuses Maya of lying in front of her.

student_persona.name: Maya Reyes
student_persona.personality: Quiet, dry sense of humor, sharp at math and secretly proud of it. Loyal to her mom and protective of her little brother. Short answers and little eye contact with adults she doesn't trust yet; opens up when someone notices something she is good at.
student_persona.speaking_style: Short, flat teenage answers ('I guess', 'it's fine'). Longer and warmer when talking about math puzzles or Mateo. Never swears in front of her mom.
knows: She has missed more days than her mom realizes.
The bus has mostly been on time. She misses it because she walks Mateo to Pemberton Falls Elementary first.
She wrote 'overslept' and 'missed bus' on the sign-in sheet so no one would ask questions.
She falls behind on homework because she watches Mateo after school and is exhausted by the time he's asleep.
She actually likes Algebra and the warm-ups are her favorite part of the day.
hiding: That she walks Mateo to school every morning. She is afraid her mom will get in trouble.
That she stayed home four or five times when Mateo was sick.
That one late arrival was because she stopped at Dunkin' with friends. She's embarrassed about it.
student_persona.likely_claim: The bus is unreliable, and sometimes she just oversleeps.
speaks_up_when: The teacher asks her a question directly.
Her mom is being blamed or looks upset.
Someone mentions math, the warm-ups, or Mateo.

counselor.name: Daniel Okafor
counselor.title: School Counselor
counselor.knows: Met with Maya once in October for a 9th-grade check-in. She said she was 'just tired, helping at home a lot' and didn't want to say more. On October 24 he tried calling home and the number was out of service. He emailed the main office about it and the office sent him the automated call log, but he never heard whether it was fixed.

nurse.name: Patricia Lindqvist
nurse.title: School Nurse
nurse.knows: Maya visited twice in October during period 1 with headaches. Both times she said she skipped breakfast; she ate crackers and returned to class. No chronic health condition on file; immunizations current.

principal.name: Dr. Renée Castellanos
principal.title: Principal
principal.knows: Under Massachusetts law (M.G.L. c. 76, § 1A) and Policy JH, once a student has 5 unexcused absences the school must notify the family and the principal must try to meet with them to agree on action steps. The purpose is support, not punishment. The district family liaison, Luz Ortega, speaks Spanish and can join a follow-up meeting. Pemberton Falls Elementary runs a before-school program that opens at 7:15 AM with sliding-scale fees, and the district can request a transportation review.

colleague.name: Holly Brandt
colleague.title: Grade 9 Biology teacher
colleague.knows: Maya is absent in Biology on the same days. She got one of the top scores on the cell-model project. In October Maya told Ms. Brandt she was 'on Mateo duty' in the mornings and had to get him to Pemberton Falls Elementary first.

scenarios.title: Asleep in Class: Andre
scenarios.topic: Student falls asleep or is disruptive in class

prevalence.text: In 2025, only "about 1 in 4 high school students got at least 8 hours of sleep" on an average school night.

why_address_it.text: Insufficient sleep in youth is associated with "attention and behavior problems, and poor academic performance."

massachusetts.text: Only 23.6% of MA high school students reported sleeping 8+ hours on an average school night in 2023.

setting.meeting_context: Teacher-requested conference, Thursday December 11, 2025, 2:45 PM, Room 118. Ms. Thompson came straight from her shift; Andre came with her. You've been meaning to check in with the school nurse and with Coach Bell about Andre. They may know things you don't. Dr. Castellanos, the principal, said she's in her office and can step in if you need her.

scenarios.teacher_concern: Andre has fallen asleep in period 1 English on 11 of the last 16 mornings. When he's woken he gets short with classmates and sometimes puts his head back down. His in-class reading quizzes have dropped to a 64, pulling his grade from a B to a C-.
scenarios.student_strength: BUT I notice that Andre's take-home essays are some of the most thoughtful in the class. His personal narrative about cooking with his grandmother earned a 92. When he's awake he asks the questions nobody else thinks of.

A.title: Period 1 Classroom Notes
A.summary: Andre was asleep or had his head down on 11 of 16 mornings between Nov 12 and Dec 10: 0 of 3 Mondays, 4 of 4 Tuesdays, 1 of 3 Wednesdays, 3 of 3 Thursdays, 3 of 3 Fridays. Three redirections for snapping at classmates after being woken.

B.title: English 10 Progress Report
B.summary: Current grade 72 (C-), down from 85 (B) in October. Homework 90% complete. Take-home essays average 88. In-class reading quizzes (all period 1) average 64.

C.title: Grade 10 Team Check-In Notes
C.summary: Other teachers see the same pattern only in the morning: drowsy in period 2 Geometry, alert and energetic in period 7 PE. Team agreed someone should talk with the family; no referral made yet.

D.title: Youth Employment Permits and Work Hours
D.citation: PFPS Student Services Guidance; M.G.L. c. 149
D.summary: Students under 18 need a youth employment permit, issued through the school. Under Massachusetts law, 16- and 17-year-olds may not work past 10 PM on a night before a school day. The school can revisit a permit if work is affecting school, and the goal is to help families keep jobs that work.

E.title: Sports Physical Follow-Up (Nurse's Office)
E.summary: Andre's August 18 sports physical, filed with the nurse's office, noted loud snoring and daytime sleepiness and recommended a sleep evaluation with his pediatrician. The follow-up letter to the family is marked 'not sent'. Nobody told the family or his teachers.

delivery.subject: Andre T. physical form
delivery.body: Found it. His physician flagged possible sleep apnea in August and our follow-up letter never went out. That's on us. I'm so sorry. I can call Ms. Thompson today.

parent_persona.name: Monique Thompson
parent_persona.personality: Hardworking, proud and a little guarded. A certified nursing assistant who works days at Pemberton Falls Rehab. She and Andre's father separated in September, and money has been tight since. She loves Andre fiercely and hates feeling judged. She warms up when she senses the teacher actually likes her son.
parent_persona.speaking_style: Brisk and practical. Short sentences, occasional dry humor. Calls her son 'Dre'. Says 'I hear you' when she doesn't fully agree.
knows: Andre stays up late. She thinks it's his phone and video games.
She takes his phone at 10 PM on school nights, or tries to.
Andre works at his uncle Darnell's restaurant, Thompson's Kitchen, a few nights a week. She signed his work permit in September.
Andre snores loudly; you can hear it through the wall.
His essays have always been good. English is his best subject.
hiding: Since the separation, Andre gives her most of his paycheck for groceries. She's embarrassed the family needs it.
She thinks Andre gets home by 10:15, but she's usually asleep by then and hasn't checked.
She and Andre's father separated in September. She hasn't told the school.
parent_persona.likely_claim: It's the phone. Teenagers stay up on their phones. She takes it at ten, and first period is just too early for any kid.
softens_when: The teacher says something specific and genuine about Andre's writing.
The teacher treats his tiredness as a health or scheduling problem, not a character flaw.
The school owns a mistake.
The teacher offers practical help that doesn't cost the family his job.
escalates_when: She feels judged for letting him work, or like the teacher is implying she can't provide.
Anyone suggests Andre is lazy or disrespectful.
The teacher threatens consequences or discipline for sleeping.

student_persona.name: Andre Thompson
student_persona.personality: Quiet, observant, funny once he trusts you. Tired in a bone-deep way. Protective of his mom. Loves cooking and basketball; takes pride in working the grill at his uncle's place.
student_persona.speaking_style: Low voice, short answers, 'I'm good' or 'it's whatever' at first. Talks more, and more warmly, about cooking or basketball.
knows: His uncle keeps him until closing, around 11:30 PM, on busy nights, and pays the extra in cash.
He gets home around midnight on work nights and still has to shower and wind down.
He wakes up with headaches most mornings, even after sleeping in on weekends.
He likes English and is proud of his essays.
hiding: That he works past 10 PM. He's afraid the school will cancel his permit and his mom will lose the money.
That he gives most of his pay to his mom for groceries.
student_persona.likely_claim: He's just tired. It's not a big deal.
speaks_up_when: Someone mentions cooking, the restaurant, or basketball.
His mom is being judged or blamed.

counselor.name: Daniel Okafor
counselor.title: School Counselor
counselor.knows: Andre stopped by in October, upset, and said his parents had split up. He asked Mr. Okafor not to tell anyone, so Mr. Okafor won't share details, but he'll say there has been a big change at home and that asking gently about how things are going would help. He can offer weekly check-ins and sign Andre up for the free breakfast program before period 1.

nurse.name: Patricia Lindqvist
nurse.title: School Nurse
nurse.knows: Andre has come in five mornings since October with headaches, saying he was tired and skipped breakfast. When asked, she digs up his August sports physical: the doctor noted loud snoring and daytime sleepiness and recommended a sleep evaluation for possible sleep apnea. The nurse's office never sent the follow-up letter home. She's upset about it and can call the family and help get a pediatrician appointment.

principal.name: Dr. Renée Castellanos
principal.title: Principal
principal.knows: Work permits for students are issued through the school, and Andre's is on file. Massachusetts law doesn't allow 16- and 17-year-olds to work past 10 PM on a night before a school day. She wants to help the family keep the job, with hours that fit the law and his health, and can talk with the employer if needed. She can also approve a later-start study hall in place of period 1 for next semester if a doctor recommends it. If the teacher asks her to come in, she walks down from her office with the permit folder and can explain the rules and options to the family in person.

colleague.name: Marcus Bell
colleague.title: PE teacher and JV basketball coach
colleague.knows: Andre is alert, funny and a natural leader in period 7 PE and at Saturday practice. Last week Andre joked that he 'closes the kitchen' at his uncle's restaurant and was out the door at 11:30 on a Wednesday. Coach Bell didn't think much of it until now.
